conversation.content: Let's design a ride-sharing service like Uber or Lyft. Users request rides, get matched with drivers, and the system handles the real-time logistics. What questions do you have?

Sure. What's the geographic scope — one city or global? What's the scale — how many ride requests per second? Do we need to support different ride types (economy, premium, shared)? What about ETA estimation and surge pricing? And what latency do we target for matching a rider with a driver?
Global service, 200 cities. 10,000 ride requests per second at peak globally. Start with just economy rides. Yes to ETA and surge pricing. Matching should happen within 10 seconds. Go ahead.

Great. Let me start with the rider experience. The user opens the app, enters their destination, and sees a fare estimate and ETA. They confirm the ride request. The system finds the nearest available driver, the driver accepts, and the user sees the driver approaching on a map in real time. During the ride, the user can track progress. At the end, the user is charged and can rate the experience. Let me design this flow.
Good overview of the rider side. Start with the architecture.

High-level architecture: The rider's app communicates with our API gateway. Behind that, key services: Ride Service (handles ride lifecycle), Location Service (tracks positions in real time), Matching Service (pairs riders with drivers), Pricing Service (fare estimates, surge), Payment Service (handles charges), and Notification Service (push notifications to the rider). The Location Service is critical — it needs to handle millions of location updates per second and provide fast geospatial queries.
Let's dig into the Location Service. How do you handle real-time location tracking at scale?

Each active rider's phone sends their GPS coordinates to the Location Service every 5 seconds. At peak, if we have a few million active riders, that's hundreds of thousands of location updates per second. The Location Service writes these to an in-memory geospatial index. I'd use a geohash-based system — divide the world into grid cells at various resolutions. Each location update maps to a geohash cell. When we need to find nearby drivers... wait, actually, the rider's location updates are less critical for matching. It's the driver locations we need for matching. Let me think about this differently.
Right — you've been focused entirely on the rider. Who else is sending location updates?

Drivers! Of course. The drivers have their own app and they're sending location updates constantly. That's actually the more important stream for matching. Available drivers are broadcasting their position so the system knows where they are. Let me rethink. The Location Service has two streams: driver locations (critical for matching) and rider locations (needed for trip tracking and ETA). The driver location stream is the one we use for the geospatial index to find nearby available drivers when a ride is requested.
So tell me about the driver's experience. What does their app look like and what are the driver-side flows?

Oh... I realize I've been designing purely from the rider's perspective. The driver side: a driver goes online and starts broadcasting their location. When a ride request comes in, the driver gets a notification with the rider's pickup location, estimated fare, and trip details. The driver has a countdown timer — maybe 15 seconds — to accept or decline. If they accept, they see navigation to the pickup point. Once they arrive, they mark 'arrived.' The rider gets in, driver starts the trip. During the trip, the driver follows navigation to the destination. At the end, they complete the trip and the fare is finalized. The driver can also see their earnings, ratings, and trip history.
Good that you've now considered the driver. Let's go to the Matching Service — how do you match a rider with a driver?

When a rider requests a ride, the Matching Service: 1) Queries the Location Service for available drivers within a radius — start with 2 km, expand if none found. The geospatial query uses the geohash index — look up the rider's geohash cell and adjacent cells. 2) From the candidate drivers, compute ETA for each using a routing engine (Mapbox or OSRM). 3) Rank drivers by ETA (shortest first), but also factor in driver rating and acceptance rate. 4) Send the ride request to the top-ranked driver. 5) If they decline or the timer expires, move to the next driver. 6) If no driver accepts within 60 seconds, notify the rider that no drivers are available.
At 10,000 ride requests per second, how does this sequential matching scale? Sending to one driver at a time seems slow.

Good point. Sequential dispatch is a bottleneck. Alternative: batch matching. Instead of matching one rider at a time, the Matching Service collects ride requests over a short window — say 2 seconds — and runs a batch optimization. It's essentially a bipartite matching problem: riders on one side, available drivers on the other, edges weighted by ETA/distance. We solve for the globally optimal assignment that minimizes total wait time. This is better than greedy sequential assignment, which can lead to suboptimal pairings. The batch window adds 2 seconds of latency but produces better overall matches.
How do you handle the case where a driver is dispatched to one rider but a closer ride request comes in before they start the trip?

That's the reassignment problem. Uber calls this 'forward dispatch.' If Driver D is heading to pick up Rider A, and a new Rider B appears much closer to Driver D's current position, we could reassign. But we need to be careful — the rider and driver have already been notified. Reassignment creates a bad user experience if done frequently. I'd only do it under strict conditions: the new match saves significant time (say 5+ minutes), the original match hasn't been active for more than 30 seconds, and neither party has been reassigned before in this request. It's a trade-off between efficiency and user trust.
Let's talk about surge pricing. How does it work technically?

Surge pricing is driven by supply-demand imbalance. The Pricing Service divides each city into hexagonal zones (using H3 geospatial indexing). For each zone, it periodically computes: demand (ride requests in the last 5 minutes) and supply (available drivers in the zone). If demand exceeds supply by a threshold, a surge multiplier kicks in — 1.2x, 1.5x, 2x, etc. The multiplier is shown to the rider before they confirm. This both discourages marginal demand and incentivizes drivers to move toward high-demand areas. The surge recalculates every minute or so.
We're running short. What about driver incentives — how do you handle the driver side of the economics?

Honestly, I hadn't fully thought through the driver economics until now. At a high level: drivers see a guaranteed minimum per trip, plus per-mile and per-minute rates. During surge, drivers earn the surge multiplier too (or a portion of it). There might be incentive bonuses — 'complete 20 rides this weekend and earn an extra $100.' These need a separate Incentives Service that tracks driver activity and triggers bonus payouts. Driver payouts happen weekly or can be daily for a fee. The system needs to track each trip's earnings, platform commission (say 20-25%), and net driver pay.
Any final thoughts?

I'd add safety features — trip sharing with contacts, an emergency button, driver background checks. Also fraud detection — fake GPS, fake rides for bonuses. And I realize my biggest gap was only thinking about the rider side for the first half. Ride-sharing is a two-sided marketplace and both sides need equal design attention. The driver supply side is arguably MORE important because without drivers, there's no service.

Exactly right. The driver side is critical and you essentially forgot it existed for the first 15 minutes. For a two-sided marketplace, you need to design both sides from the start. The matching and pricing work was solid once you got going. Thank you.

strengths: Strong matching algorithm design — batch optimization and reassignment policy
Good surge pricing mechanism with H3 hexagonal zones
Solid geospatial indexing approach with geohash
weaknesses: Completely forgot the driver side for the first half of the interview
No database schema discussion — what does the rides table look like?
Zero failure handling — what if a driver's phone loses signal mid-trip?
No caching strategy discussed for location data or fare estimates
Treated ride-sharing as a one-sided consumer product instead of a two-sided marketplace
